extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners reviewing §101 guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing patent claim subject-matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 (MPEP §2106): how to determine whether claims merely recite judicial exceptions (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas) and whether additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application or provide 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to apply a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim (or combination of elements) must do 'more than simply stat[e] the [judicial exception] while adding the words 'apply it''. Claims that amount to nothing more than an instruction to apply the abstract idea using a generic computer do not render an abstract idea eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Alice (quoting Mayo) and Benson: recitation of a computer that merely tells the user to 'apply' the exception on the computer is insufficient. Examiners should carefully consider each claim on its merits and evaluate overlapping considerations (improvement, particular machine/transformation, well-understood/routine/conventional) to determine whether an element is more than mere instructions to apply an exception. Note: examiners should not evaluate the well-understood, routine, conventional consideration in the Step 2A Prong Two analysis because that consideration is evaluated in Step 2B. See MPEP § 2106.07(a) for formulating eligibility rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recites only idea or outcome (no details of how solution is accomplished)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome i.e., fails to recite details of how a solution to a problem is accomplished. Recitation of claim limitations that attempt to cover any solution to an identified problem with no restriction on how the result is accomplished and no description of the mechanism for accomplishing the result does not integrate a judicial exception into a practical application or provide significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Result-oriented or highly functional claims that merely state a desired outcome are equivalent to saying 'apply it.' Cases: Electric Power Group; Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec; Internet Patents v. Active Network. In contrast, claiming a particular solution or a particular way to achieve an outcome may integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more. Example: IV v Capital One (dynamic XML modifications lacked specific steps and were ineligible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invoking computers/machinery merely as a tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim invokes computers or other machinery merely as a tool to perform an existing process. Use of a computer or other machinery in its ordinary capacity (e.g., to receive, store, or transmit data) or adding a general purpose computer does not integrate a judicial exception into a practical application or provide significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/cases: Affinity Labs (cellular telephone), TLI Communications (telephone unit and server used in ordinary capacity), Alice, Gottschalk v. Benson. Claiming only improved speed or efficiency due to a general-purpose computer is insufficient. In contrast, a claim that improves computer capabilities or improves an existing technology may integrate the exception (see McRO, Enfish). See MPEP §§ 2106.04(d)(1) and 2106.05(a) for improvements to computer/technology discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity vs generality of application (breadth of claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: The particularity or generality of the application of the judicial exception: a claim having broad applicability across many fields of endeavor may not provide meaningful limitations that integrate the judicial exception into a practical application or amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that generically recite an effect or claim every mode of accomplishing that effect are effectively adding 'apply it.' Cases: Internet Patents v. Active Network (maintaining state of data in online form without mechanism), O'Reilly v. Morse, The Telephone Cases. Limitations that confine the exception to a particular, practical application may amount to significantly more (see BASCOM example where filtering at a specific ISP location with customizable features was meaningful).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the additional elements add more than insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception. 'Extra-solution activity' are activities incidental to the primary process or product that are merely a nominal or tangential addition to the claim and include pre-solution and post-solution activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts (Parker v. Flook, Mayo) hold that adding post-solution or well-understood conventional activity does not amount to an inventive concept. Examples: pre-solution data gathering (obtaining credit-card info), post-solution output (printing a report). Evaluation overlaps with particular machine/transformation, well-understood/routine/conventional, and field-of-use considerations; examiners should consider all relevant considerations before determining insignificance. See MPEP § 2106.05(g) for more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extra-solution consideration: whether the limitation is well-known
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the extra-solution limitation is well known (i.e., token/known techniques are token extra-solution activity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Bilski (well-known random analysis techniques), Flook (use with existing surveying techniques), IV v Erie (use of well-known XML tag). Because this overlaps with the conventional/well-understood consideration, it should not be considered in the Step 2A Prong Two extra-solution analysis (it is evaluated in Step 2B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extra-solution consideration: whether the limitation is significant
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the limitation is significant (i.e., it imposes meaningful limits on the claim such that it is not nominally or tangentially related to the invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a limitation meaningfully confines the claim it may not be 'insignificant extra-solution activity.' Cases: Ultramercial (restricting public access to media found insignificant), Apple v. Ameranth (certain electronic menu features found significant/insignificant in context). This factor is considered in Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extra-solution consideration: whether the limitation amounts to necessary data gathering/outputting
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the limitation amounts to necessary data gathering and outputting (i.e., all uses of the recited judicial exception require such data gathering or data output).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the extra activity is merely the kind of data collection/outputting that any use of the exception would need, it is likely insignificant. Cases: Mayo (measuring metabolites), OIP Technologies, CyberSource. The MPEP provides lists of activities courts have found to be mere data gathering (clinical tests, testing system responses, presenting offers and gathering statistics, obtaining transactions info, updating activity logs, determining biomarker levels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples: selecting a particular data source or type as insignificant
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting a particular data source or type of data to be manipulated (e.g., limiting a database index to XML tags; taking orders from only certain customer types; selecting information for power-grid environments) can be an insignificant extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases/examples: IV v Erie (XML tags); Ameranth (table-based or drive-through orders); Electric Power Group v. Alstom (power-grid data selection); Ultramercial (restricting public access to view ads). Such limitations may be both extra-solution activity and field-of-use limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples: insignificant application (post-solution activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-solution activities that do not integrate the exception (e.g., cutting hair after selecting a hairstyle; printing/downloading generated menus) are examples of insignificant application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases/examples: In re Brown (cutting hair after hairstyle determination); Ameranth (printing/downloading menus). These are treated as nominal additions that do not make the claim patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant computer implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some cases identify insignificant computer implementation as an example of insignificant extra-solution activity: using generic computing components in a conventional manner does not add significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Fort Properties v. American Master Lease; Bancorp Services v. Sun Life (insignificant computer implementation). Other cases treat such limitations as mere instructions to apply the exception (see MPEP §2106.05(f)). See MPEP §2106.05(f) and §2106.05(g) for treatment and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of use / technological environment limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the additional elements amount to more than generally linking the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use. Merely indicating a field of use or technological environment does not make a claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court example: Parker v. Flook (limiting formula to petrochemical/oil-refining fields was insufficient). Diamond v. Diehr shows contrast when specific limitations act in concert to transform a process. Affinity Labs v. DirecTV is an example where limiting to cellular telephones was insufficient. Examiners should consider that 'technological environment' and 'field of use' are interchangeable for eligibility analysis. This consideration overlaps with extra-solution activity; examiners must explain why such a limitation does not meaningfully limit a claim in a rejection. See list of field-of-use examples in MPEP §2106.05(h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological solution to a technological problem may integrate a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claim recites a technological solution to a technological problem (specific configuration, manipulation, or methods that override conventional behavior), the additional elements can be more than mere instructions to apply an exception and thus integrate into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: DDR Holdings (manipulating Internet interactions to yield a desired result that overrode routine/conventional sequences), BASCOM (filtering tool at a specific ISP location with customizable features), Thales Visionix (particular inertial sensor configuration and raw-data usage). Examiners should look for specificity that describes how the technological result is achieved rather than a mere result-oriented limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner explanation requirement for eligibility rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: When claim limitations do not meaningfully limit the claim (mere 'apply it', insignificant extra-solution activity, merely linking to a field of use), examiners should explain in an eligibility rejection why those limitations do not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application or provide significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example explanatory approach: explain that implementing an abstract idea on a generic computer does not integrate the idea (as in Alice). Provide reasoning showing why added steps are nominal/tangential, well-known, or merely link to a field of use. See MPEP §2106.07(a) for additional guidance on formulating subject matter eligibility rejections.
